# Judges 17 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter, together with chapter 18, is an appendix to the Book of Judges, not chronologically placed after Samson but occurring early in the period, shortly after Joshua's death. It shows the internal religious and moral breakdown of Israel — self-styled worship and self-determined service — in contrast to the external enemies emphasized in chapters 3–16.

- **Ellicott** notes that both appendices (chs. 17–18 and 19–21) serve "the purpose of showing the social anarchy, religious confusion, and moral degradation" of the period, and that the presence of Jonathan grandson of Moses (Judg 18:30) and Phinehas grandson of Aaron (Judg 20:28) shows these events happened shortly after Joshua's death. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Precept Austin** cites G. Campbell Morgan: "The events here recorded must have taken place closely following the death of Joshua." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_17_commentary]
- **Gill** says it "relates the first rise of idolatry in Israel after the death of Joshua." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]
- **Constable**: "Whereas chapters 3–16 record Israel's struggles with her external enemies, chapters 17–21 document the internal conditions of the nation that made her so weak. In chapters 17–18 we see Israel abandoning God." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]

---

## v. 1 — "Now a man named Micah from the hill country of Ephraim…"

- **Name**: The Hebrew is *Micayehu*, meaning "Who is like Yahweh?" — deeply ironic since he becomes an idolater. Ellicott observes that the very name "seems to show that he had been trained by pious parents." The shortened form *Micah* is used throughout the rest of the story. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Location**: The hill country of Ephraim is in central Palestine, not far from Shiloh where the true tabernacle stood (cf. Judg 18:31). Micah thus had no practical need for a private shrine. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]
- **Setting**: David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that Judges 17–18 "present a detailed example of the spiritual confusion and sin in Israel during the days of the judges." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-17/]
- **Precept Austin** adds: "Judges 17–21 deal with the deadly enemy which is internal, our fallen flesh." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_17_commentary]

---

## v. 2 — "The eleven hundred shekels of silver that were taken from you… I took it."

- **The theft**: Micah stole an enormous sum from his own mother. Constable notes that 1,100 shekels could have sustained a person for a lifetime (compare the Levite's yearly wage of 10 shekels in v. 10). It weighed about 28 pounds of silver. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]
- **The curse**: The mother had uttered an oath/curse (*alah*) against the thief (cf. Lev 5:1, the "voice of swearing"). Ellicott points out that Micah "is terrified into confession by his mother's adjuration. He shows throughout a singular mixture of superstition and ignorance." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Walter Kaiser** (cited at Precept Austin) explains: "Curses were taken too seriously in those days… When Micah heard his mother cut loose with this oath, he immediately confessed that he was the thief. He obviously feared the consequences of the oath." The mother's blessing was likely meant to "mitigate, if not nullify, the negative effect of the curse." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_17_commentary]
- **Matthew Henry** (from excerpt): "The love of money made Micah so undutiful to his mother as to rob her, and made her so unkind to her son, as to curse him. Outward losses drive good people to their prayers, but bad people to their curses." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/17.htm]
- **Gill**: The mother "reversed the curse, and pronounced a blessing on him… and that without reproving him for his sin, rejoicing to hear of her money again." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]
- **Guzik**: The confession was likely motivated by fear of the curse, not genuine repentance. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-17/]

---

## v. 3 — "I wholly dedicate the silver to the LORD for my son's benefit, to make a graven image and a molten idol."

- **Dedication**: The mother says, "I had wholly dedicated" (Hebrew *hiqdashti* — "consecrating, I consecrated"). Ellicott says this can mean either "I have now consecrated it" as a thanksgiving for its restoration, or "I had done so before it was stolen." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Gill** explains she "doubtless meant the true God; for she had no intention to forsake him, but to worship him in and by these images, and which she designed for the use of her son and his family, that they might not go so far as Shiloh to worship at the tabernacle there." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]
- **Guzik**: "Some people believe this was an image of a false god (such as Baal or Ashtoreth). Others believe that it was an image representing Yahweh. Either way, God strictly forbade such an image." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-17/]
- **The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary** (StudyLight) observes: "She professes to have devoted the whole of the money to the service of God's house, yet when coming to the decision as to how much shall be given for that purpose, she gives really less than one-fifth of the whole to that service." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-17.html]
- **Constable**: "Micah had evidently learned dishonesty at home." The mother "stole from God as her son had stolen from her." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]

---

## v. 4 — "She took two hundred shekels of silver and gave them to a silversmith…"

- **Only 200 of 1,100 shekels** went to the images. The remaining 900 shekels were apparently kept by the mother or spent on other cultic items (the ephod, teraphim, shrine). Gill notes that Kimchi thought the 200 shekels were the silversmith's fee and the 900 were the material, while others think the opposite. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]
- **Pesel and Massekah**: Ellicott says these "are the very words used in the curse against idolaters in Deuteronomy 27:15." Some take the two terms as hendiadys — a single image with both carved and cast elements. Others see two distinct objects. The *massekah* may have been a pedestal for the *pesel*. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Ellicott's Excursus on Calf-Worship**: He argues that "the calf-worship was a violation not of the first, but of the second commandment." The calf was a "recognised cherubic emblem" and images made by Micah and later Jeroboam "were not idols in the ordinary sense of the word, but were intended as symbols of the one God." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Constable**: The graven image (*pesel*) occurs "almost exclusively in relation to the golden calves that Aaron made (Exodus 32:4) and King Jeroboam made (1 Kings 12:28–30)." Micah's mother likely intended it to represent either Yahweh or the animal pedestal on which deities were imagined to stand. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]

---

## v. 5 — "Now this man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and some household idols, and ordained one of his sons as his priest."

- **"House of gods"** (Hebrew *Beth Elohim*): JFB calls it "a domestic chapel, a private religious establishment of his own." Ellicott notes it could equally mean "a house of God." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm] / [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/17.htm]
- **Ephod**: A priestly garment, probably an imitation of the high priest's ephod, perhaps used for divination (cf. Gideon's ephod in Judg 8:27). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]
- **Teraphim (household idols)**: Gill says these were "a sort of household gods, like the Lares and Penates of the Romans, and by which consultations were made." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html] Ellicott traces their use in Israel from Genesis 31:19 through to Josiah's reformation (2 Kgs 23:24). They "involved a violation of the second commandment." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Ordaining his son**: The Hebrew phrase is "filled the hand" — the technical term for priestly consecration (Exod 28:41). JFB says: "The assumption of the priestly office by any one out of the family of Aaron was a direct violation of the divine law (Nu 3:10; 16:17; De 21:5; Heb 5:4)." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/17.htm]
- **Guzik**: "By each of these actions, Micah did everything he could to set up a rival religion in Israel… This was a completely man-originated and man-centered religion." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-17/]
- **Gaebelein** (typological reading): "Here is a man-made god, a man-made worship and a man-made priest. Such is the state of ritualistic Christendom." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/judges-17.html]

---

## v. 6 — "In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes."

- This refrain appears four times in the final chapters (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25). It is the narrator's editorial comment.
- **JFB**: "From want of a settled government, there was no one to call him to account. No punishment followed any crime." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/17.htm]
- **Gill**: "No supreme magistrate, judge, or ruler, Joshua being dead and Caleb also, and the elders contemporary with them." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]
- **Constable**: "Even though there was not yet a human king, Yahweh reigned as Israel's monarch from heaven. Since His people paid no attention to His authority by disregarding His Law, Israel was practically without a king." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]
- **Guzik**: "This refers to the radical individualism that marked the time of the judges. People looked to self for their guide to morality and ethics… they measured it only by their own eyes." He adds that this "follow-your-heart" mentality is celebrated in modern culture but leads only to ruin. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-17/]
- **Ellicott**: The editorial note "shows that these narratives were written, or more probably edited, in the days of the monarchy." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Precept Austin** ties the verse to Psalm 11:3: "If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?" and notes that the solution is a King — ultimately Jesus Christ. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_17_commentary]

---

## v. 7 — "And there was a young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah who had been residing within the clan of Judah."

- A Levite, but not of the Aaronic priestly line. Bethlehem was not a Levitical city, so his residence there was irregular.
- **Ellicott** notes the startling revelation in Judges 18:30 that this young man was a grandson (or descendant) of Moses through Gershom. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **"Of the family of Judah"**: Ellicott says this may refer to Bethlehem (the city being in Judah) or to the Levite himself, meaning he was "ranked in civil matters as belonging to that tribe" since he lived there. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Gill**: He was "by his father's side a Levite, and by his mother's side… of the tribe of Judah." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]
- **Constable**: "His disregard for God's will is obvious in his choice to live somewhere other than where God told the Levites to live." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]

---

## vv. 8–9 — The Levite leaves Bethlehem, travels, and comes to Micah's house.

- **Why he left**: Gill suggests the lack of a central magistrate meant Levites were not receiving their due tithes, forcing him "to go abroad, and seek for a livelihood where he could get it." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html] Ellicott compares this to Nehemiah's day: "the portions of the Levites had not been given them… they were fled every one to his field" (Neh 13:10–11). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Constable** calls him "shiftless" and quotes Block: "Unlike Abraham, who also set out for an unknown destination but who went with a keen sense of the calling of God, this person is shiftless. He has no passion for God, no sense of divine calling, no burden of responsibility. He is a 'laid back' professional minister following the path of least resistance." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]
- **Guzik**: This Levite "had cities to live in and a place established by God for him to minister. Instead, he wanted to do what was right in his own eyes and went about offering himself as a priest for hire." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-17/]

---

## v. 10 — "Stay with me… be my father and priest, and I will give you ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions."

- **"Father and priest"**: Ellicott says "the title 'father' is here ecclesiastical, like 'papa,' 'pope,' etc., and this title was given to spiritual directors" (cf. 2 Kgs 2:12; 6:21). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm] Gill adds: "a father to instruct him in the knowledge of divine things; so prophets were called fathers, and their disciples their sons." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]
- **The wage**: Ten shekels a year plus room and board. Ellicott remarks: "Thus the grandson of Moses became priest of an idolatrous worship at a salary of 25s. a year!" [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Guzik**: "The Levite was a perfect example of a hireling, someone who served God (or an idol) for what it could give him, instead of serving to glorify the LORD." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-17/]
- **Gaebelein** sees a typical application: "Religious service is so much reduced to a commercial basis. And there is the delusion of thinking that the Lord must surely bless and give prosperity." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/judges-17.html]

---

## v. 11 — "The Levite agreed to stay with him, and the young man became like a son to Micah."

- Gill notes the mutual satisfaction: Micah "used as kindly and tenderly, as if he had been one of his own children; so strong were the affections of Micah to him." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]
- Ellicott says the phrase "was unto him as one of his sons" is "added by way of reflection on his subsequent ingratitude" (i.e., his later betrayal when the Danites arrived in ch. 18). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]

---

## v. 12 — "Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in his house."

- **"Ordained"** literally "filled the hand" — the same idiom used for consecrating Aaron's sons. JFB: "This act of consecration was not less unlawful for Micah to perform than for this Levite to receive." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/17.htm]
- **Guilt of the Levite**: Guzik says "the Levite was guiltier than Micah was… because the Levite was at least supposed to know the word of God." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-17/]
- Gill calls it "a very daring piece of presumption in them both; in Micah, to take upon him to consecrate a priest, who was himself of the tribe of Ephraim; and in the young man, to suffer himself to be put into such an office, which did not belong to him." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]
- **Constable**: "Judges 17:1–6 stress the sin of self-styled worship. Judges 17:7–13 emphasize the folly of self-determined service." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]

---

## v. 13 — "Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest."

- **Superstitious confidence**: Micah believed having a genuine Levite (as opposed to his own son) legitimized his worship and guaranteed God's blessing. JFB: "The removal of his son, followed by the installation of this Levite into the priestly office, seems to have satisfied his conscience… This expression of his hope evinces the united influence of ignorance and superstition." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/judges/17.htm]
- **Gill**: "By this it appears, that notwithstanding the idolatry he had fallen into, he had not utterly forsaken the Lord, but worshipped him in and by his images; there was a mixture of the worship of God, and of the worship of images." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]
- **Guzik**: "Micah's confidence was just as false as his consecration was. They were both based on superstition, not on God's word… Micah was utterly sincere – but totally wrong. Sincerity is nice but gets you nowhere if it is not coupled with truth." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-17/]
- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary**: "What miserable logic does an unrenewed man show, when trying to make out a favourable case for himself as regards his personal religion." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-17.html]
- **Ellicott** notes the irony: "In this anticipation we find a very little further on that he was rudely undeceived" (ch. 18 when the Danites steal his idols and priest). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]
- **Gaebelein**: The scene typifies "the delusion of thinking that the Lord must surely bless and give prosperity" — a "manufactured priesthood for manufactured gods, all covered with a fair name of orthodoxy." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/judges-17.html]

---

## Denominational Distinctives & Traditions

Because the available searched sources showed broad agreement on Judges 17 (the chapter is universally read as a negative example of self-made religion), there are few sharp denominational disagreements. What follows are the distinct emphases traceable in the sources found:

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik)** emphasizes application to contemporary worship: man-centered religion versus God-centered worship, the danger of "sincerity without truth," and the warning against following one's own instincts in faith. Guzik ties "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" directly to modern culture's "follow your heart" mentality. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-17/]

- **Reformed Baptist (Gill)** stresses the sovereignty of God in law and judgment, the unlawfulness of Micah's actions under the Mosaic law, and the role of the civil magistrate in restraining sin. Gill explicitly connects the absence of a king to the lack of anyone to "take cognizance of his sin, and restrain him from it, or punish him for it according to the law of God." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-17.html]

- **Anglican/Moderate Protestant (Ellicott)** provides detailed historical and textual notes, including the Excursus on Calf-Worship (arguing the calves were symbolic of Yahweh, not foreign gods, making the violation of the second commandment rather than the first) and the Excursus on Teraphim. He also notes that the events must be dated early by the presence of Moses' grandson. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/17.htm]

- **Brethren/Evangelical (Gaebelein)** reads the chapter typologically: Micah's setup represents "ritualistic Christendom" with "a man-made god, a man-made worship and a man-made priest." He sees in the hired Levite a picture of hirelings and a man-made priesthood corrupting Christianity, with the repeated "no king in Israel" pointing forward to the need for Christ as King. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/judges-17.html]

- **Dispensational/Evangelical (Constable)** notes the "Bethlehem trilogy" connection (Judges 17–18, 19–21, and Ruth) as tracing "the roots of the Davidic dynasty" and observes that the monarchy itself later failed because kings also "did what was right in their own eyes." He identifies three trends of the apostasy: religious syncretism (vv. 1–5), moral relativism (v. 6), and extreme materialism (vv. 7–13). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-17.html]

- **Matthew Henry (Nonconformist/Puritan)** characteristically draws moral lessons: "The love of money made Micah so undutiful to his mother as to rob her… This woman's silver was her god, before it was made into a graven or a molten image." He traces the root: "Every man did that which was right in his own eyes, and then they soon did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/17.htm]

- **Holiness/Methodist (Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary)** highlights conscience, self-deception, and the gradual nature of idolatry: "Idolatry begins with those who are not upright in moral conduct," and warns that image worship, though begun with intention to worship the true God, "insensibly leads after a time to the worship of the image itself." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-17.html]

**Note**: Lutheran (LCMS / 1517.org), specific Catholic/Orthodox, and modern scholarly sources were not retrieved due to search limits. No prosperity/Word of Faith readings of this chapter were found in the sources searched.
